claims.text: The as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy has a dual-phase microstructure consisting of a disordered FCC matrix and a B2 intermetallic phase.
The as-cast alloy exhibits high ductility and homogeneous deformation.
Aging at approximately 600°C produces a peak-ordered state with an L12 ordering fraction greater than 0.45 in the FCC matrix.
The antiphase boundary energy is maximized or strongly elevated in the highly ordered state produced at 600°C.
Elevated antiphase boundary energy energetically prohibits dislocation cross-slip.
Suppression of cross-slip confines dislocations to specific slip planes and produces planar slip.
The B2/FCC phase boundaries are jagged and contain serration-like teeth.
Planar slip bands impinge on the jagged B2/FCC interfaces.
Stress concentration at interface serrations, coupled with the inability of dislocations to bypass or blunt the interface by cross-slip, causes crack nucleation and brittle fracture.
Tensile elongation after peak ordering at 600°C will be less than 5%.
Aging at 750°C lowers the L12 ordering fraction below approximately 0.30 through thermal disordering.
The reduced order at 750°C lowers the antiphase boundary energy.
Lower antiphase boundary energy at 750°C restores dislocation cross-slip.
Aging at 750°C increases the width of disordered transition zones at the B2/FCC interfaces.
At 750°C, the interface morphology relaxes or ductile amorphous-like transition zones form.
Tensile elongation after aging at 750°C will recover to greater than 20%.
Antiphase boundary energy can be inferred from superlattice streaking intensity and dislocation dissociation width.
The brittle transition occurs when the L12 ordering fraction exceeds approximately 0.45.
The return to ductility occurs when the L12 ordering fraction falls below approximately 0.30.
Simple phase decomposition without ordering effects would be indicated by dislocation pile-ups, whereas the proposed mechanism predicts no such pile-ups.

contradictions.description: The mechanism explicitly states that high ordering and high APBE cause planar slip, while jagged interfaces convert that planar slip into concentrated damage. Therefore, observing planar slip after flattening the interface is predicted by the mechanism and does not falsify the proposed ordering-interface coupling, contrary to falsification rule (1). A valid flattening test would instead assess whether cracking or brittle response is suppressed while planar slip remains.

The hypothesis refers to f_L2 at 750°C, whereas all other fields define the relevant order as L12. This is most likely a notation error but leaves the identity of the measured ordering fraction formally inconsistent.
